entry.description: Or 'Unsolicited Bulk Email', this means that the recipient has not granted verifiable permission for the message to be sent and that the message is sent as part of a larger collection of messages, all having a functionally comparable content. This IOC refers to resources which make up spam infrastructure, for example, harvesters like address verification, URLs in spam emails, etc.

tlctc.note: Indicator: attacker infrastructure, not a victim event; serves #9 if a message carries a lure (link, attachment or request) to a person. Ask: Does the message carry a lure? Plain advertising involves no step against an IT system.

entry.description: Bullying, harassment or discrimination of somebody, e.g., cyber stalking, racism or threats against one or more individuals.

tlctc.note: No cluster: harm to a person through content; no step against an IT system.

entry.description: Child Sexual Exploitation (CSE), sexual content, glorification of violence, etc.

tlctc.note: No cluster: harmful or illegal content; no step against an IT system.

entry.description: System infected with malware, e.g., a PC, smartphone or server infected with a rootkit. Most often this refers to a connection to a sinkholed command and control server.

tlctc.note: <enabler> → #7 (R-EXEC); RSIT does not record the preceding step. Ask: How did the code arrive and start?

entry.description: Command and control server contacted by malware on infected systems.

tlctc.note: Indicator: attacker infrastructure, not a victim event; serves #7 (R-EXEC) if on the infected systems that contact it.

entry.description: URI used for malware distribution, e.g., a download URL included in fake invoice malware spam or exploit kits (on websites).

tlctc.note: Indicator: attacker infrastructure, not a victim event; serves #7 (R-EXEC) if a victim runs the downloaded code; #3 (R-ROLE) if an exploit kit on the site exploits the visiting browser or client before the code runs. Ask: Is the hosting site itself compromised? That is a separate path against its owner.

entry.description: URI hosting a malware configuration file, e.g., web injects for a banking trojan.

tlctc.note: Indicator: attacker infrastructure, not a victim event; serves #7 (R-EXEC) if on the infected systems that load the configuration.

entry.description: Attacks that send requests to a system to discover weaknesses. This also includes testing processes to gather information on hosts, services and accounts. This includes fingerd, DNS querying, ICMP, SMTP (EXPN, RCPT, etc) port scanning.
Observing and recording of network traffic (i.e. wiretapping).

tlctc.note: One of: #1 if capture with designed functions (promiscuous mode) where the attacker already has access; #5 (R-MITM) if the attacker holds a position on the communication path + [DRE: C]. Ask: Where was the capture point?

entry.description: Gathering information from a human being in a non-technical way (e.g., using lies, tricks, bribes, or threats).

An attempt to compromise a system or to disrupt any service by exploiting vulnerabilities with a standardised identifier such as CVE name (e.g., using a buffer overflow, backdoor, cross site scripting)

tlctc.note: Attempt, success not asserted: #2 (R-ROLE) if the flawed component serves the attacker (server role); #3 (R-ROLE) if the flawed component consumes attacker content (client role). A blocked attempt is a near miss, not an incident. Ask: Did it succeed? If so, classify the record under the matching Intrusions value.

entry.description: Multiple brute-force login attempts (including guessing or cracking of passwords). This IOC refers to a resource, which has been observed to perform brute-force attacks over a given application protocol.

tlctc.note: Attempt, success not asserted: #4 (R-CRED). A blocked attempt is a near miss, not an incident. Ask: Did any attempt authenticate? If so, classify the record under Unprivileged or Privileged Account Compromise.

entry.description: An attack using an unknown exploit.

tlctc.note: Attempt, success not asserted: #2 (R-ROLE) if the flawed component serves the attacker (server role); #3 (R-ROLE) if the flawed component consumes attacker content (client role). A blocked attempt is a near miss, not an incident. Ask: Did it succeed? If so, classify the record under the matching Intrusions value.

entry.description: Compromise of a system where the attacker has gained administrative privileges.

tlctc.note: One of: #4 (R-CRED) if administrative credentials were applied; their acquisition is a separate step before; #2 (R-ROLE) if a flaw in a privileged component was exploited (local privilege escalation); #1 if privileges were reached through designed functions or a misconfiguration. Ask: How were administrative privileges obtained?

entry.description: Compromise of a system using an unprivileged (user/service) account.

tlctc.note: <acquisition> → #4 (R-CRED); RSIT does not record the preceding step. Ask: How was the credential obtained?

entry.description: Compromise of an application by exploiting (un)known software vulnerabilities, e.g., SQL injection.

tlctc.note: One of: #2 (R-ROLE) if the application serves the attacker (server role), e.g. SQL injection; #3 (R-ROLE) if the application processes attacker-supplied content (client role). Ask: Did the application serve the attacker or consume attacker content?

entry.description: Compromise of a system, e.g., unauthorised logins or commands. This includes attempts to compromise honeypot systems.

tlctc.note: One of: #4 (R-CRED) if an unauthorised login with a credential; #1 if commands run through designed functions; #2 (R-ROLE) if a flaw in a server-role component was exploited. Ask: Which act gave the attacker the system? RSIT also files attempts on honeypots here; a failed attempt is a near miss, not a compromise.

entry.description: Physical intrusion, e.g., into a corporate building or data centre.
Denial of Service attack, e.g., sending specially crafted requests to a web application which causes the application to crash or slow down.

tlctc.note: One of: #6 (R-SPECIFIC) if volume or intensity exhausts finite resources; #2 (R-SPECIFIC) if an implementation defect crashes or hangs a server-role component; #3 (R-SPECIFIC) if an implementation defect crashes or hangs a client-role component + [DRE: A]. Ask: Flaw or capacity?

entry.description: Distributed Denial of Service attack, e.g., SYN flood or UDP-based reflection/amplification attacks.

tlctc.note: #6 (R-SPECIFIC) + [DRE: A].

entry.description: Software misconfiguration resulting in service availability issues, e.g., DNS server with outdated DNSSEC Root Zone KSK.

tlctc.note: No cluster: Failure / external event (operational risk).

entry.description: Intentional actions maliciously threatening to, attempting to or actually damaging a system or component with the aim of disrupting the availability of a service. These can happen both at logical and physical levels, from malicious firewall rules dropping all traffic, to wire-cutting, bomb threats or arson.

tlctc.note: One of: #8 if physical damage, e.g. cutting wires or arson; #1 if logical damage by an actor outside any grant, e.g. malicious firewall rules; how the actor reached the system is a separate step; no cluster, Abuse of Rights, if an entitled actor acting within the grant (R-SCOPE); no cluster (a threat with no act against the system, e.g. a bomb threat) if nothing was done to an IT system. Ask: Physical or logical? Was the actor acting within their access rights?

entry.description: An outage caused, for example, by air conditioning failure or natural disaster.

tlctc.note: No cluster: Failure / external event (operational risk).

entry.description: Unauthorised access to information, e.g., by abusing stolen login credentials for a system or application, intercepting traffic or gaining access to physical documents.

tlctc.note: Data state [DRE: C], not a cause; possible causes: #4 (R-CRED) if stolen login credentials were applied; #5 (R-MITM) if traffic was intercepted; #8 if physical documents were accessed. Ask: Which step gave the access?

entry.description: Unauthorised modification of information, e.g., by an attacker abusing stolen login credentials for a system or application, or ransomware encrypting data. Also includes defacements.

tlctc.note: Data state [DRE: I], not a cause; possible causes: #4 (R-CRED) if stolen login credentials were applied; #7 (R-EXEC) if ransomware encrypted the data (DRE Ac: present but unusable); #7 (R-EXEC) if a defacement placed attacker content (as ATT&CK T1491; DRE Ii). Ask: Which step changed the data?

entry.description: Loss of data caused by, for example, hard disk failure or physical theft.

tlctc.note: Data state [DRE: Av], not a cause; possible causes: no cluster, Failure / external event, if a hard disk or other failure; #8 if physical theft (confidentiality may be lost as well). Ask: Failure or theft?

entry.description: Leaked confidential information, e.g., credentials or personal data.

tlctc.note: Data state [DRE: C], not a cause. Ask: Which step exposed the information?

entry.description: Using resources for unauthorised purposes including profit-making ventures, e.g., the use of email to participate in illegal profit chain letters or pyramid schemes.

tlctc.note: No cluster: Abuse of Rights (operational risk). Ask: Was the access legitimately granted? If it was gained by an attack, the use is the outcome of that attack's path.

entry.description: Offering or installing copies of unlicensed commercial software or other copyright protected materials (also known as Warez).

tlctc.note: No cluster: intellectual-property infringement; no step against an IT system (compliance risk: a BRE entered by a normative edge).

entry.description: Type of attack in which one entity illegitimately impersonates the identity of another in order to benefit from it.

tlctc.note: One of: #9 if the impersonation deceives people; #4 (R-CRED) if the impersonator authenticates to a system as the entity. Ask: Were people deceived, or did a system authenticate the impersonator?

entry.description: Masquerading as another entity in order to persuade the user to reveal private credentials. This IOC most often refers to a URL, which is used to phish user credentials.

tlctc.note: #9 + [DRE: C] → #4; RSIT does not record the following step. Ask: Were the credentials used?

entry.description: Publicly accessible services offering weak cryptography, e.g., web servers susceptible to POODLE/FREAK attacks.

tlctc.note: Exposure: a state with no step and no SRE; enables #5 if an attacker on the path can read or downgrade the channel (as CWE-326, CWE-327, CWE-757).

entry.description: Publicly accessible services that can be abused for conducting DDoS reflection/amplification attacks, e.g., DNS open-resolvers or NTP servers with monlist enabled.

tlctc.note: Exposure: a state with no step and no SRE; enables #6 if against the victim the reflected traffic is sent to; #1 if the amplifier's designed response function is abused.

entry.description: Potentially unwanted publicly accessible services, e.g., Telnet, RDP or VNC.

tlctc.note: Exposure: a state with no step and no SRE; enables #4 (R-CRED) if credentials are applied to the exposed login; #1 if designed functions of the exposed service are used.

entry.description: Publicly accessible services potentially disclosing sensitive information, e.g., SNMP or Redis.

tlctc.note: Exposure: a state with no step and no SRE; enables #1 if unauthenticated designed functions disclose data (as CWE-306) (potential DRE C).

entry.description: A system which is vulnerable to certain attacks, e.g., misconfigured client proxy settings (such as WPAD), outdated operating system version, or cross-site scripting vulnerabilities.

tlctc.note: Exposure: a state with no step and no SRE; enables #2 (R-ROLE) if an outdated or flawed server-role component; #3 (R-ROLE) if an outdated or flawed client-role component; #5 if a proxy auto-discovery misconfiguration (WPAD) lets an attacker take the communication path.

entry.description: All incidents which don't fit in one of the given categories should be put into this class or the incident is not categorised.

tlctc.note: Unresolved (?): no cluster can be defended from the value. Ask: What happened? Reclassify once the record is understood.

entry.description: The categorisation of the incident is unknown/undetermined.

tlctc.note: Unresolved (?): no cluster can be defended from the value. Ask: What happened? Reclassify once the record is understood.

entry.description: Meant for testing.

tlctc.note: Excluded: test record, not an event.

predicates.description: Software that is intentionally included or inserted in a system for a harmful purpose. A user interaction is normally necessary to activate the code.

A successful compromise of a system or application (service). This can have been caused remotely by a known or new vulnerability, but also by an unauthorised local access. Also includes being part of a botnet.

By this kind of an attack a system is bombarded with so many packets that the operations are delayed or the system crashes. DoS examples are ICMP and SYN floods, Teardrop attacks and mail-bombing. DDoS often is based on DoS attacks originating from botnets, but also other scenarios exist like DNS Amplification attacks. However, the availability also can be affected by local actions (destruction, disruption of power supply, etc.) – or by Act of God, spontaneous failures or human error, without malice or gross neglect being involved.

Besides a local abuse of data and systems the information security can be endangered by a successful account or application compromise. Furthermore attacks are possible that intercept and access information during transmission (wiretapping, spoofing or hijacking). Human/configuration/software error can also be the cause.
Open resolvers, world-readable printers, vulnerabilities apparent from scans, anti-virus signatures not up-to-date, etc.

All incidents which don't fit in one of the given categories should be put into this class. If the number of incidents in this category increases, it is an indicator that the classification scheme must be revised.
